objective: By the end of this lesson you can describe the five elements of planning instructional activity the PTS lists (objectives and standards for a course of training, the building-block theory of learning, the requirements for a training syllabus, the purpose and characteristics of a lesson plan, and how a scenario-based lesson is developed), and use them to lay out an instrument rating course, write an instrument lesson plan and turn it into a scenario-based lesson an examiner would accept.
why: The AIH says the instructor should know how to create and use lesson objectives and lesson plans, and that the learning that takes place is a direct result of the instructor's active lesson preparation, delivery, observation and assessment [[25:145|AIH 7-1]]. The PHAK adds that a structured training program and a formal course syllabus are crucial for effective flight training [[1:38|PHAK 1-23]]. Whenever Area I is tested, the PTS NOTE tells the evaluator to select at least this Task, Tasks E and F and one other Task [[FAA-S-8081-9E:23|PTS Area I NOTE]], so expect to explain it aloud and to show plans of your own.

An organized outline for a single instructional period: what to do, in what order and with what procedure [[25:151|AIH 7-7]].

chunks.title: Planning from the course down to the lesson

body.p: This lesson follows the five items the PTS lists for Planning Instructional Activity [[FAA-S-8081-9E:25|PTS I.G]]. The CFI lesson FI.I.C teaches the same AIH chapter inside a broader CFI ACS Task. This lesson goes deeper on each planning step and uses an instrument rating course as the running example. The teaching methods inside a lesson are in FOI.I.C and FOI.I.D, and the postflight assessment is in FOI.I.E.

The AIH opens Chapter 7 with Susan and Bill, who are flying a lesson scenario: a short cross-country to practice landings at a nontowered airport, then home to Class C airspace. Susan notices the ceiling lowering and the crosswind increasing. Bill thinks they can stay longer, but instead of saying so he asks her questions: has the situation changed, what about the weather, how can we get more information, what about fuel, schedule, equipment and pilot capability? She decides to go home and practice there. It is a good plan based on situational awareness and risk management, so Bill agrees, and in the postflight critique Susan leads the discussion of her decisions [[25:145|AIH 7-1]].

That is the point of this Task. The FAA now places greater emphasis on the instructor as teacher and mentor: the instructor should understand how to create and use lesson objectives and lesson plans, and the learning that takes place is a direct result of the instructor's active lesson preparation, delivery, observation and assessment [[25:145|AIH 7-1]]. Chapter 7 organizes planning around four topics, course of training, blocks of learning, training syllabus and lesson plans, and then shows how to bring SBT, ADM and risk management into the lesson [[25:145|AIH 7-1]].
**Four terms, from biggest to smallest** [[25:107|AIH 5-4]]:

bullets: **Course of training:** a complete series of studies leading to a specific goal, such as a certificate of completion, graduation or an academic degree. It can be as narrow as the additional training for high-performance airplanes [[25:107|AIH 5-4]].
**Curriculum:** for pilot training, usually the courses for the various pilot certificates and ratings [[25:107|AIH 5-4]].
**Syllabus:** a summary or outline of one course of study that generally contains multiple lessons, with a description of each lesson including objectives and completion standards [[25:107|AIH 5-4]].

**Lesson plan:** a detailed plan for how one lesson will be conducted: objectives, organization of the material, teaching aids, instructor and learner actions, and evaluation criteria and completion standards [[25:107|AIH 5-4]].

check.q: Your examiner asks, "What is the difference between a curriculum, a syllabus and a lesson plan?" Give one line for each.
check.a: A curriculum is the set of courses for the various certificates and ratings. A syllabus outlines one course, lesson by lesson, with each lesson's objectives and completion standards. A lesson plan is the detailed plan for conducting one lesson [[25:107|AIH 5-4]].

chunks.title: Objectives and standards for a course of training

body.p: **Objectives and standards come first.** A determination of objectives and standards precedes instruction. Many instructors use a commercially developed syllabus, and its objectives are their starting point [[25:108|AIH 5-5]].

**The overall course objective.** It is usually well established. A broad, overall objective of any pilot training course is to qualify the learner to be a competent, efficient, safe pilot for the operation of specific aircraft types under stated conditions [[25:108|AIH 5-5]]. The general standards come from rules and publications: eligibility, knowledge, proficiency and experience requirements are in the regulations, and the standards are published in the applicable ACS or PTS [[25:108|AIH 5-5]].

**Instrument example.** For an instrument-airplane course, 14 CFR 61.65 already sets much of the frame: the aeronautical knowledge areas for the ground training or home-study course [[60:250|14 CFR 61.65(b)]], the eight areas of operation the flight training must include, from preflight preparation to postflight procedures [[60:251|14 CFR 61.65(c)]], and the experience the applicant must log, such as 40 hours of actual or simulated instrument time with 15 of them from an authorized instructor who holds an instrument-airplane rating [[60:251|14 CFR 61.65(d)(2)]]. The AIH calls this the basic planning already provided by the knowledge and proficiency requirements in the regulations, approved school syllabi and published texts [[25:145|AIH 7-1]].

callout.text: Do not stop at the minimum. ACS/PTS standards are limited to the most critical job tasks, and certification tests do not represent an entire training syllabus [[25:108|AIH 5-5]]. Professional instructors should not limit their objectives to the minimum published requirements: successful instructors teach not only how, but also why and when, and build ADM and risk management into each lesson [[25:108|AIH 5-5]]. The IFH says the same for instruments: the rating certifies only that the pilot complied with the minimum experience requirements, can plan and fly IFR and basic instrument maneuvers, and showed acceptable skill and judgment, and training should develop the judgment to use the skills within the pilot's own limits [[23:11|IFH viii]].

body.p: **Standards** include a description of the desired knowledge, behavior or skill in specific terms, with conditions and criteria. When a learner performs to well-defined standards, evidence of learning is apparent [[25:108|AIH 5-5]]. Standards are easy to set for the cognitive and psychomotor domains, but harder for the affective domain of attitudes, beliefs and values [[25:108|AIH 5-5]].

**At every level of the course.** Set appropriate objectives and standards for the overall course, for the separate ground and flight segments, and for each stage of training [[25:147|AIH 7-3]]. Lesson completion standards should gradually reach or exceed those in the ACS/PTS before final checkride preparation, because the ACS/PTS is a testing tool, not a teaching tool [[25:171|AIH 9-1]].

check.q: A new CFII tells you, "My course objective is simple: pass the instrument checkride." What is missing?
check.a: Certification tests cover only the most critical tasks and are not a whole syllabus, and good instructors do not stop at the minimum published requirements: they teach how, why and when, with ADM and risk management in each lesson [[25:108|AIH 5-5]]. Objectives and standards are also needed for the ground and flight segments and each stage [[25:147|AIH 7-3]].

body.p: Aviation training uses two types of objectives: performance-based and decision-based [[25:108|AIH 5-5]]. **Performance-based objectives** set measurable, reasonable standards for the learner's desired performance. They may also be called behavioral, performance, instructional or educational objectives; all refer to the behavior of the learner [[25:108|AIH 5-5]]. They state the level of performance the learner must show before moving to the next stage, and they should be clear, measurable and repeatable and mean the same thing to any knowledgeable reader [[25:108|AIH 5-5]].

body.p: Conditions and criteria may be refined as you write. In the AIH's own example they change slightly as the objective is developed, and that is exactly how real objective development happens [[25:109|AIH 5-6]].

**Levels and domains.** Objectives apply to all three domains of learning (cognitive, affective and psychomotor) and should include the desired level of learning [[25:108|AIH 5-5]]. The verbs show the level: define, identify and label for rote; describe, estimate or explain for understanding; determine, develop and solve for application [[25:65|AIH 3-14]]. Above all, clearly defined objectives that the learner understands are essential, whatever the teaching technique [[25:108|AIH 5-5]].

callout.text: Use the ACS as a source of objectives. ACS documents give the instructor specific performance objectives based on the standards for a certificate or rating [[25:109|AIH 5-6]]. Test items should be content valid (the maneuver closely mimics what actual flying requires) and criterion valid (the completion standards reflect acceptable standards in actual flight) [[25:109|AIH 5-6]]. Application: an approach flown to the published missed approach point tests a real skill; a drill that never happens in IFR flight would not be content valid.

check.q: Rewrite this instrument objective so it can be measured: "The learner will have knowledge of VOR tracking."
check.a: "Knowledge of" cannot be measured very well [[25:108|AIH 5-5]]. Example: in the training airplane under a view-limiting device, using the en route chart (conditions), the learner intercepts and tracks an assigned radial (description) within the course limits set for this stage (criteria) [[25:108|AIH 5-5]] [[25:109|AIH 5-6]].

chunks.title: Decision-based objectives, and what objectives do for the plan

body.p: **Decision-based objectives** specifically develop pilot judgment and ADM skills. Improper pilot decisions cause a significant percentage of all accidents and the majority of fatal accidents [[25:110|AIH 5-7]]. These objectives facilitate a higher level of learning and application: with dynamic and meaningful scenarios, the instructor teaches the learner how to gather information and make informed, safe and timely decisions [[25:110|AIH 5-7]].

As the learner progresses through higher levels of performance and understanding, shift the training focus toward decision-based objectives. They rely on a more dynamic training environment, are ideally suited to SBT and teach critical thinking such as risk management and ADM [[25:108|AIH 5-5]]. They do not replace maneuver training: maneuvers that need repetition may still be taught in concentrated settings and are then integrated into realistic flight situations [[25:110|AIH 5-7]]. It has been found that SBT learners fly as well as or better than learners trained only with maneuvers, and the same data suggest they make better decisions [[25:110|AIH 5-7]].

body.p: **Other uses of objectives.** Objectives help you design the whole lesson plan: their parts suggest the elements of the lesson and the schedule, and they already name the equipment and the instructor and learner actions. By listing the criteria, you have already written the lesson's completion standards [[25:110|AIH 5-7]]. Objectives also give the learner the big picture and what is expected, which removes a significant source of uncertainty and frustration [[25:110|AIH 5-7]].

callout.text: Application: in an instrument course, write both kinds for each stage. A partial panel stage might pair a performance-based objective (control the airplane on partial panel within stated limits) with a decision-based one (recognize a failed attitude indicator, tell ATC and decide whether to continue). The RMH says risk management training is more effective when integrated with the knowledge, risk and skill requirements of the ACS [[30:59|RMH A-1]].

check.q: Your instrument learner now flies approaches well in the practice area. What should change in your objectives, and why?
check.a: Shift the focus toward decision-based objectives taught in realistic scenarios. They suit a learner at higher levels of performance and build ADM and risk management [[25:108|AIH 5-5]], while the approach skill is integrated into realistic flights [[25:110|AIH 5-7]].

body.p: **Blocks come after objectives.** After the overall training objectives are set, the next step is to identify the blocks of learning that make up the total objective [[25:146|AIH 7-2]]. The AIH compares the course to a pyramid: some blocks are buried in the structure and never appear on the surface, but each is an integral and necessary part of it. The blocks are not isolated subjects but essential parts of the whole [[25:146|AIH 7-2]].

bullets: **Find the foundation early.** Identifying the foundation blocks early is essential, because piloting needs many blocks assembled in their proper relationships [[25:146|AIH 7-2]].
**Master, then combine.** The learner masters the blocks individually and progressively combines them with related blocks until their sum meets the overall objective [[25:146|AIH 7-2]].

**No frills.** Check that each block is an integral part of the structure. Extraneous blocks are expensive frills, especially in flight instruction, and detract from the final objective [[25:146|AIH 7-2]].

**Consistent, measurable blocks.** Blocks should be fairly consistent in scope and be units of learning that can be measured and evaluated, not a sequence of periods of instruction. Private pilot training might be split into the knowledge and skills for solo, for solo cross-country and for the certificate [[25:146|AIH 7-2]].

**Confidence.** Completing each block normally gives the learner a boost in self-confidence. Broken into smaller blocks, a large goal becomes manageable instead of seeming unobtainable [[25:146|AIH 7-2]].
**Simple to complex.** Humans learn from the simple to the complex: a learner masters normal landings before short-field and soft-field landings [[25:146|AIH 7-2]].

body.p: **Know the learner's background.** By becoming familiar with the learner's aviation background, you can plan the sequence of blocks. A helicopter pilot moving to airplanes understands speed control but may not know how to achieve it in an airplane, so you plan blocks that build on what he already knows [[25:147|AIH 7-3]]. This fits Bruner's advice to teach from the known to the unknown, because humans learn best when relating new knowledge to existing knowledge [[25:55|AIH 3-4]].

check.q: Why does the AIH call extra blocks of instruction "expensive frills"?
check.a: Every block should be an integral part of the structure. Extraneous blocks cost money, especially in flight instruction, and detract from completing the final objective [[25:146|AIH 7-2]].

body.p: Instrument training is a clear case of building blocks. The IFH says the two fundamental skills of attitude instrument flying, instrument cross-check and instrument interpretation, are learned separately and in deliberate sequence, and a measure of proficiency is the ability to integrate them into smooth, positive control [[23:143|IFH 6-10]]. It adds that the sequential nature of the learning process requires each element of knowledge and skill to be learned and applied in the right manner at the right time [[23:11|IFH viii]].

The IFH's Instrument Training Lesson Guide is arranged in a logical learning sequence using the building-block technique, and each lesson includes ground training that fits its flight portion. Learners should master each lesson's objective before advancing, and the lessons should be arranged to take advantage of each learner's knowledge and skills [[23:342|IFH B-1]].

body.p: **Scenarios grow in blocks too.** The AIH teaches decision-making in three phases: first the stick-and-rudder skills, then scenarios that bring in hazards, risk and resources, and finally more complex scenarios with several safety-of-flight issues. Scenarios start simply and progress in complexity and intensity as the learner can handle more workload [[25:30|AIH 1-26]].

**Ground, device, airplane.** In an integrated program the instructor first teaches the knowledge for a task such as the ILS on the ground, then adds the psychomotor skills in a simulator, and moves to the aircraft once the learner is proficient in the device [[25:174|AIH 9-4]].

callout.text: When a block will not stick, go back a block. The AIH's example is a learner struggling with normal landings: delay short-field landings and review slow flight, which gives the learner a chance to do well and builds the skills needed for the landings [[25:147|AIH 7-3]]. Application: if holding falls apart, return to the tracking block before adding more clearance changes.

check.q: Your new learner logged 15 hours of hood work in a training device two years ago. Where in the IFH guide do you start, and why?
check.a: With Lesson 1, the ground and flight evaluation of the learner's knowledge and performance [[23:342|IFH B-1]]. Knowing his background lets you plan blocks that build on what he already knows [[25:147|AIH 7-3]], and the guide's lessons should take advantage of each learner's knowledge and skills [[23:342|IFH B-1]].

chunks.title: Requirements for developing a training syllabus

body.p: Instructors need a practical guide that keeps training in a logical sequence and makes sure all requirements are completed and properly documented; a well-organized, comprehensive syllabus does this [[25:147|AIH 7-3]]. The PHAK warns that part 61 sets the minimum experience and knowledge training but does not say how training is organized, so an instructor who fails to organize it can cost the learner time and money through repetitious training. One way to avoid that, it says, is a flight instructor with a well-documented training syllabus [[1:34|PHAK 1-19]].
**What every syllabus should be and contain:**

bullets: An abstract or digest of the course of training [[25:147|AIH 7-3]].
Blocks of learning to be completed in the most efficient order [[25:147|AIH 7-3]].

Fairly brief, yet comprehensive enough to cover essential information, usually in outline form, lesson by lesson. Some syllabi add tables of recommended training time for each lesson and the overall minimum time [[25:147|AIH 7-3]].
Well-defined objectives and standards for each lesson, the overall course, the separate ground and flight segments, and each stage [[25:147|AIH 7-3]].
Optional details on how to use it and on the training and reference materials, such as textbooks, websites, video, exams, briefings and instructional guides [[25:147|AIH 7-3]].
Risk management instruction unique to each stage, phase or training element, with increasingly subtle risks as training goes on [[25:149|AIH 7-5]].
Where needed: recommended class time, study materials, the sequence of training, the study assignment for the next lesson and explanatory notes on specific lessons [[25:150|AIH 7-6]].

body.p: **Three parts in every syllabus lesson.** Each ground or flight lesson should include an objective, content and completion standards, and more than one objective often applies to a single flight lesson [[25:148|AIH 7-4]] [[25:149|AIH 7-5]]. Ground lessons concentrate on the cognitive domain, flight lessons emphasize the psychomotor domain, and in both the learner's attitude toward safety, ADM and judgment, the affective domain, should be a major concern [[25:147|AIH 7-3]] [[25:148|AIH 7-4]].

callout.text: Part 141 schools. Syllabi for approved schools contain specific information outlined in 14 CFR parts 141 and 142; syllabi for other training may lack details such as enrollment prerequisites, planned completion times and the checks and tests for each stage [[25:147|AIH 7-3]]. Under part 141, the course's training syllabus must include the prerequisites for enrolling in the ground and flight portions; a detailed description of each lesson with its objectives, standards and planned time for completion; what the course is expected to accomplish in student learning; the expected accomplishments and standards for each stage; and the checks and tests used to measure accomplishment at each stage [[60:785|14 CFR 141.55(c)(7)]].

check.q: Figure 7-3 is a private pilot flight lesson. What three parts does it show, and what in it shows instrument work already being built in?
check.a: Lesson objectives, content and completion standards [[25:149|AIH 7-5]]. The note requiring a view-limiting device for 0.2 hours of dual instrument time and the (IR) items show instrument reference work woven in; IR marks maneuvers flown by both visual and instrument references in integrated instruction [[25:149|AIH 7-5]] [[25:150|AIH 7-6]].

chunks.title: Running example: an instrument rating syllabus

body.p: The IFH says its Appendix B curriculum gives guidance on the minimum training for adding an instrument rating to a private or commercial pilot certificate, whatever training method is chosen [[23:11|IFH viii]]. Flight instructors may use it to develop lesson plans, and it should be cross-referenced with the IFH and the instrument practical test standards for a comprehensive program [[23:342|IFH B-1]].

**What the guide gives you, and what you add.** Each lesson lists ground training topics and flight training items, but no objectives, completion standards or times [[23:342|IFH B-1]] [[23:344|IFH B-3]]. To meet the AIH's syllabus requirements, you add them [[25:147|AIH 7-3]] [[25:148|AIH 7-4]].

Credit limits: 20 hours in a full flight simulator or flight training device (30 under part 142), 10 in a BATD or 20 in an AATD when the device and the training are FAA approved and an authorized instructor gives it, and 20 hours total in all devices except under part 142 [[60:252|14 CFR 61.65(h)]] [[60:253|14 CFR 61.65(i)]] [[60:253|14 CFR 61.65(j)]]
Records and endorsements

Spaces to record completion, grades and times, which support endorsements and test recommendations [[25:150|AIH 7-6]]. The guide's last note: the recommending instructor ensures the applicant meets the part 61 training, knowledge, experience and endorsement requirements [[23:344|IFH B-3]]

callout.text: Put the learner's real trip in the syllabus. Scenarios can be tailored to local weather and terrain and are most effective when they replicate the environment the learners will most likely meet [[25:157|AIH 7-13]]. Application: plan the cross-country lessons toward the destination the learner actually wants to fly to.

check.q: The school owner hands you the IFH lesson guide and says, "That's our instrument syllabus." What is still missing?
check.a: The guide gives lesson topics in a building-block order [[23:342|IFH B-1]], but a syllabus also needs well-defined objectives and standards for each lesson, the course, the ground and flight segments and each stage [[25:147|AIH 7-3]], with completion standards in each lesson [[25:148|AIH 7-4]].

chunks.title: Using the syllabus: a flexible guide

body.p: **A guide, not a cage.** Any practical training syllabus needs to be flexible and should be used primarily as a guide. Under 14 CFR part 61, the order of training can and should be altered to suit the learner's progress and special circumstances; previous experience or different rates of learning often call for some changes or repetition [[25:147|AIH 7-3]]. It should also adapt to weather, aircraft availability and scheduling changes without disrupting the teaching process or suspending training [[25:147|AIH 7-3]].

**Departing from the order.** When you depart from the syllabus order, it is your responsibility to consider how the relationships of the blocks are affected, as in the AIH's example of reviewing slow flight before adding short-field landings [[25:147|AIH 7-3]].

**At a certificated school.** Each approved course should follow a syllabus specifically approved by the FAA. Compliance with it is a condition for graduation, it should be referred to throughout the course, and both the instructor and the learner should have a copy. Even so, it should not be so stringent that it cannot adapt to individual needs [[25:147|AIH 7-3]]. The PHAK adds that part 141 schools must document the curriculum and have their courses approved, while part 61's advantage is flexibility to tailor lessons to the individual [[1:34|PHAK 1-19]].

**Records.** A syllabus can be a checklist that required training is done, usually with boxes or spaces next to each item; some add grades and ground and flight times. Accurate records keep the learner and instructor informed and serve as a basis for endorsements and test recommendations [[25:150|AIH 7-6]]. Most syllabi introduce each procedure or maneuver in one lesson and review it in later lessons [[25:150|AIH 7-6]], and a well-constructed syllabus already holds much of what a lesson plan needs: objectives, content and completion standards [[25:151|AIH 7-7]].

check.a: Under part 61 the syllabus is a guide whose order can and should change to suit her progress, and when you depart from it you consider how the blocks relate [[25:147|AIH 7-3]]. Telling her why keeps the big picture clear and removes a source of frustration [[25:110|AIH 5-7]].

chunks.title: The purpose of a lesson plan

body.p: A **lesson plan** is an organized outline for a single instructional period. It is a necessary guide because it tells the instructor what to do, in what order and with what procedure, and one should be prepared for each training period [[25:151|AIH 7-7]].

**In writing.** A mental outline of a lesson is not a lesson plan. Another instructor should be able to take your plan and know how to conduct the same period, and a written plan can be analyzed for adequacy and completeness [[25:151|AIH 7-7]]. Lesson plans also make good recordkeeping forms for the training record, with a checklist of what was completed, the date, the instructor's signature, time flown and comments [[25:151|AIH 7-7]].

**Purpose.** Lesson plans are designed to assure that each learner receives the best possible instruction under the existing conditions, and they help instructors keep a constant check on their own activity and the learner's. Developing them means, in effect, that you have taught the lesson to yourself before teaching it to a learner [[25:152|AIH 7-8]]. An adequate lesson plan, properly used, should:

bullets: Assure a wise selection of material and the elimination of unimportant details [[25:152|AIH 7-8]].
Make certain that due consideration is given to each part of the lesson [[25:152|AIH 7-8]].
Aid the instructor in presenting the material in a suitable sequence for efficient learning [[25:152|AIH 7-8]].
Provide an outline of the teaching procedure to be used [[25:152|AIH 7-8]].
Serve as a means of relating the lesson to the objectives of the course of training [[25:152|AIH 7-8]].
Give the inexperienced instructor confidence [[25:152|AIH 7-8]].
Promote uniformity of instruction regardless of the instructor or the date on which the lesson is given [[25:152|AIH 7-8]].

body.p: **A training folder.** Keep lesson plans, training requirements, instruction received, part 61 requirements met, solo endorsements and other training information in one folder for each learner, and keep the records at least 3 years [[25:152|AIH 7-8]].

callout.text: Ask your plan seven questions. What goes in, and what stays out? Does each part get its due? In what order? Taught how? Tied to which course objective? Would a new instructor feel ready? Would any instructor, any day, teach it the same way? Those are the seven things an adequate lesson plan should do [[25:152|AIH 7-8]].

check.q: The examiner asks, "You have taught this lesson fifty times. Why write a plan?"
check.a: A mental outline is not a lesson plan. Written, it can be checked for completeness and another instructor can teach from it [[25:151|AIH 7-7]]. It keeps you from getting off track, omitting essential points or adding irrelevant material [[25:153|AIH 7-9]], and it promotes uniform instruction [[25:152|AIH 7-8]].

chunks.title: Characteristics of a well-planned lesson, and using the plan

body.p: **The planning cycle.** After the objective is determined, research the subject as the objective defines it, decide the method of instruction and a useful lesson planning format, then decide how to organize the lesson and select support material. The final steps are assembling training aids and writing the lesson plan outline. One technique is to write the beginning and ending first, then complete the outline and revise it; a lesson plan is a working document [[25:152|AIH 7-8]].

body.p: **Using a lesson plan properly:**

bullets: **Be familiar with it.** Study each step of the plan and know as much related information as possible [[25:153|AIH 7-9]].

**Use it as a guide.** It keeps you from getting off track, omitting essential points or introducing irrelevant material; a carefully reviewed lesson plan is the most certain means of teaching success [[25:153|AIH 7-9]].

**Adapt it to the class or learner.** If the plan is not working, change the approach. A flight lesson plan should fit the learner's background, experience and ability; it may be modified considerably in flight, or even abandoned in favor of review [[25:153|AIH 7-9]].
**Revise it periodically,** for example when instructional aids change, regulations change, or new manuals and textbooks come out [[25:153|AIH 7-9]].

body.p: **Formats.** Format and style depend on several factors, such as the subject matter and the teaching method: plans may be simple for one-on-one training and elaborate for large, structured classroom lessons. All should include objectives, content to support them and completion standards, though completion standards may be called assessment, review and feedback, performance evaluation or a similar term [[25:153|AIH 7-9]]. Aviation lessons involve all three domains, and their objectives usually reach at least the application level [[25:153|AIH 7-9]].

callout.text: Commercially developed lesson plans are acceptable for most training, including use by flight instructor applicants on their practical tests. Even well-designed preprinted plans may need changes, so adapt them to the learner and the situation [[25:153|AIH 7-9]].

check.q: Halfway through a planned holding lesson, you see that your learner has lost the basic cross-check. What does the AIH say about the plan?
check.a: Adapt it. A flight lesson plan may have to be modified considerably in flight because of poor mastery of essential elements, and in some cases abandoned in favor of review [[25:153|AIH 7-9]].

body.p: The AIH's traditional lesson plan teaches wind drift control. It lists the objective, completion standards and content: a preflight discussion, review items, an introduction with a demonstration of turns around a point and S-turns, and a postflight discussion [[25:154|AIH 7-10]]. The instructor reviews, explains, demonstrates and has the learner practice until the maneuver is consistent within set limits, but at the end the learner can only practice the maneuver with the instructor's help [[25:153|AIH 7-9]].

Here is the same traditional format applied to Lesson 6 of the IFH guide, partial panel operations. **This sample is this lesson's own example, not an FAA lesson plan.** Only the ground and flight training items come from the IFH guide; the objective, completion standards, review choice and briefing items were written for this lesson, using the AIH format.

What it does not do is put the skill inside a real flight with decisions to make. That is the job of the SBT lesson plan, which presents the objectives in a scenario [[25:154|AIH 7-10]] [[25:155|AIH 7-11]].

chunks.title: How a scenario-based lesson is developed

body.p: **Why SBT.** Improper pilot decisions cause a significant percentage of all accidents and the majority of fatal accidents in light single- and twin-engine aircraft. SBT challenges the learner with a variety of flight scenarios to improve decision-making: managing the resources in the flight deck, considering hazards, exercising sound judgment and making timely decisions [[25:154|AIH 7-10]]. Because people develop cognitive skills through active interaction with the world, the effective instructor uses the maneuver- or procedure-based approach but presents the objectives in a scenario [[25:155|AIH 7-11]].
**Step 1: pre-scenario planning.** For SBT to be effective, the instructor and learner establish:

head: Flight scenario
Nonflight scenario
rows: Scenario destination(s) [[25:155|AIH 7-11]]
Narrative of the task goal [[25:155|AIH 7-11]]
Desired learning outcomes
Desired learning outcomes
Desired level of learner performance
Desired level of learner performance
Possible inflight scenario changes
Possible scenario changes

body.p: **Step 2: write the story.** For the flight instructor, a good scenario tells a story that begins with a reason to fly, because a pilot's decisions differ with the motivation to fly [[25:120|AIH 5-17]]. Adapt it to the aircraft, its flight characteristics and the likely flight environment, and always require real-time decisions in a realistic setting [[25:57|AIH 3-6]]. Scenarios can be tailored for local weather and terrain and work best when they replicate the environment learners will most likely meet [[25:157|AIH 7-13]].

**Step 3: test it.** A good scenario is not a test, will not have one right answer, does not offer an obvious answer, should not promote errors, and should promote situational awareness and opportunities for decision-making [[25:120|AIH 5-17]]. Chapter 1 adds that it engages all three learning domains, is interactive and requires time-pressured decisions [[25:31|AIH 1-27]]. Chapter 3 adds a clear set of objectives, tailoring to the learner's needs and using the nuances of the local environment [[25:82|AIH 3-31]].

**Step 4: plan the outcomes.** Understand in advance which outcomes are positive and which are negative, and give the learner freedom to make both good and poor decisions without jeopardizing safety [[25:120|AIH 5-17]]. That does not mean letting the learner make an unsafe decision or commit an unsafe act [[25:31|AIH 1-27]].

**Step 5: lay it out.** The AIH's SBT lesson plan lists the type of training, the maneuver or training objective, the scenario, completion standards, possible hazards or considerations, mitigation strategies and resources, flying the scenario and a postflight review. Every hazard or consideration should be addressed with some mitigating strategy or resource [[25:156|AIH 7-12]]. Its completion standard is not a maneuver tolerance: the learner can explain a safe arrival at any nontowered airport in any wind condition [[25:156|AIH 7-12]].

**Step 6: let the learner lead, then debrief.** Scenarios should be planned and led by the learner, except for the first flight or two or until the learner has the needed skills [[25:57|AIH 3-6]]. On arrival the learner makes the decisions, with guidance and feedback as needed, followed by a discussion of what was done, why, the consequences, other courses of action and how it applies elsewhere [[25:155|AIH 7-11]]. The postflight review typically begins with learner self-critique, and the instructor leads with questions that generate reflective thinking [[25:156|AIH 7-12]]. Collaborative assessment is used whenever the learner has completed a scenario [[25:182|AIH 9-12]]; FOI.I.E covers it in depth.

check.q: Your learner asks why your scenario has no single right answer. What do you tell her?
check.a: Real situations rarely have one. A good scenario is not a test: it will not have one right answer or an obvious one, and it should give her opportunities to make decisions [[25:120|AIH 5-17]].

callout.text: Keep every simulated failure and scenario change safe. Know the good and poor outcomes in advance and let the learner choose, but never let the learner make an unsafe decision or commit an unsafe act [[25:31|AIH 1-27]]. Place boundaries around scenarios so the transitions between scenarios and traditional training are as efficient as possible, and when you revise a scenario from learner feedback, do not further complicate it unless highly justified [[25:157|AIH 7-13]].

body.p: **Explaining the Task aloud.** The PTS says instructional knowledge includes developing scenario-based lessons and using learner-centered grading [[FAA-S-8081-9E:10|PTS Use of the PTS]], and it tells evaluators to test application and correlation with scenario-based questions where possible [[FAA-S-8081-9E:14|PTS Evaluator Responsibility]]. A strong answer follows one thread from top to bottom: the course objective and standards, the blocks and their order for this learner, what the syllabus contains, today's lesson plan, and how today's maneuver lives inside a scenario.

scenario.title: An instrument course for Raj
scenario.setup: You are a new CFII at a part 61 flight school. Raj is a private pilot with 260 hours who owns a fixed-pitch four-seat airplane with a GPS navigator and a single alternator. He wants an instrument rating so he can fly to client meetings about two hours away, often in winter and over hilly terrain. Last year he flew 12 hours under the hood with another instructor, almost all of it the same ILS again and again, and he has no syllabus or training records except his logbook. He can fly twice a week, and the school's training device is free on bad-weather days. The chief instructor asks you to plan his whole course and bring his first lesson plan to your next meeting.

questions.q: What do you write first, and what should the overall course objective say?
questions.a: Objectives and standards come before instruction [[25:108|AIH 5-5]], and they then determine the lesson plans, test items and levels of learning [[25:145|AIH 7-1]]. The overall objective is to make Raj a competent, efficient, safe pilot for his airplane under stated conditions, with standards from the regulations and the ACS/PTS but not limited to the minimums: teach why and when, with ADM and risk management in each lesson [[25:108|AIH 5-5]]. Then set objectives for the ground and flight segments and each stage [[25:147|AIH 7-3]].

questions.q: How do his 12 hours of repeated ILS practice change the blocks you plan?
questions.a: Learn his background first so the blocks build on what he knows [[25:147|AIH 7-3]]; the IFH guide starts with a ground and flight evaluation [[23:342|IFH B-1]]. Repeating one approach is blocked practice, which scores well during practice but retains worse than random practice [[25:78|AIH 3-27]]. Check the foundation blocks, cross-check and interpretation, before the approach blocks, since those skills are learned in sequence and then integrated [[23:143|IFH 6-10]] [[25:146|AIH 7-2]].

questions.q: What must your syllabus for Raj contain?
questions.a: A brief but comprehensive digest of the course, the blocks in the most efficient order, lesson-by-lesson objectives and standards, standards for the course, segments and stages, and the materials he will use [[25:147|AIH 7-3]], plus risk management for each stage [[25:149|AIH 7-5]]. Build in the experience he must log, such as 40 hours of instrument time with 15 from an instrument instructor and the 250 nautical mile IFR cross-country [[60:251|14 CFR 61.65(d)(2)]].

questions.q: It storms on the day of his first approach lesson. Do you cancel training?
questions.a: No. The syllabus should adapt to weather, aircraft availability and schedules without suspending training [[25:147|AIH 7-3]]. Teach the approach knowledge on the ground and the procedure in the training device, then move to the airplane once he is proficient in the device [[25:174|AIH 9-4]].

questions.q: What goes into his first lesson plan, and how will you use it in the airplane?
questions.a: Objectives, content and completion standards [[25:153|AIH 7-9]], written so another instructor could teach from it [[25:151|AIH 7-7]], with a short review and a scope he can master [[25:152|AIH 7-8]]. Use it as a guide, fit it to his background, and change it or even drop it for review if he lacks an essential element [[25:153|AIH 7-9]].

questions.q: Later in the course, how do you build an SBT lesson around his real trips?
questions.a: Set the destination, learning outcomes, performance level and possible changes with him [[25:155|AIH 7-11]], start the story with his real reason to fly [[25:120|AIH 5-17]], and include instrument risks such as night, low IMC, icing and his single alternator [[25:189|AIH 10-5]]. Let him plan and decide [[25:155|AIH 7-11]], then debrief starting with his self-critique [[25:156|AIH 7-12]] and use collaborative assessment [[25:182|AIH 9-12]].

skills.do: Explain the purpose and characteristics of a lesson plan the way an examiner expects, then walk through one of your own instrument lesson plans and show where each characteristic appears.
skills.practice: Take one lesson from the IFH guide [[23:343|IFH B-2]] and write it in the traditional format with objectives, content and completion standards [[25:153|AIH 7-9]]. Check it against the seven characteristics [[25:152|AIH 7-8]] [[25:153|AIH 7-9]]. Present it to a study partner in under five minutes and have them ask "But what if...?" questions, which show where the conditions need work [[25:109|AIH 5-6]].

skills.do: Describe step by step how you develop a scenario-based lesson, with an instrument example: pre-scenario planning, the story, the good-scenario tests, hazards and mitigations, the learner's role and the postflight review.
skills.practice: Convert your traditional plan into the SBT format of Figure 7-7 [[25:156|AIH 7-12]]. Role-play it with another applicant as the learner, since role playing grows in importance as SBT is emphasized [[25:100|AIH 4-7]], and finish with a replay, reconstruct, reflect and redirect debrief [[25:136|AIH 6-5]] [[25:137|AIH 6-6]].

quiz.q: Your examiner asks what an instructor determines first when planning instruction around a course of training. Which answer matches the AIH?
options: The lesson plans, which are then grouped into blocks
The training aircraft, which limits what can be taught
The objectives and standards, which shape the rest
The test items, which are worked backward into lessons
quiz.why: The instructor plans content around the course by determining objectives and standards, which in turn determine lesson plans, test items and levels of learning [[25:145|AIH 7-1]]. Lesson plans come last, after the blocks and the syllabus [[25:146|AIH 7-2]] [[25:151|AIH 7-7]].

quiz.q: A syllabus objective reads: "The learner will be aware of holding procedures." What is the main problem?
options: It names no instrument approach procedure
"Aware of" cannot be measured very well
It uses a verb from the psychomotor domain
It gives too many criteria for one lesson
quiz.why: Phrases like "knowledge of" and "awareness of" cannot be measured very well and should be avoided; describe something measurable instead [[25:108|AIH 5-5]]. The objective has no criteria at all, so "too many criteria" is wrong [[25:109|AIH 5-6]].

quiz.q: Reviewing your holding objective, a colleague keeps asking, "But what if the GPS is not working?" What does that tell you?
options: The criteria are too strict for this stage of training
The verb shows the wrong level of learning
The conditions are confusing and need work
The objective should be decision-based
quiz.why: When a reader asks "But what if...?", it is a good sign the conditions are confusing and need clarification [[25:109|AIH 5-6]]. Criteria measure accomplishment; equipment and limits belong in the conditions [[25:109|AIH 5-6]].

quiz.q: Which describes a block of learning the way the AIH wants it?
options: A unit that can be measured and evaluated
A set number of periods of instruction in a row
A subject taught apart from all others
An extra topic added to keep interest high
quiz.why: Blocks should be fairly consistent in scope and be units of learning that can be measured and evaluated, not a sequence of periods of instruction [[25:146|AIH 7-2]]. They are not isolated subjects, and extraneous blocks are expensive frills [[25:146|AIH 7-2]].

quiz.q: Your part 61 instrument learner is struggling with holding. What does the AIH say about changing the syllabus order?
options: Never; the order is a condition of completion
Only after a failed stage check shows the need
It can and should change, with the blocks in mind
Only if the FAA approves a revised syllabus
quiz.why: Under part 61, the order of training can and should be altered to suit the learner's progress, and the instructor must consider how the relationships of the blocks are affected [[25:147|AIH 7-3]]. Compliance as a condition of graduation applies to approved courses at certificated schools [[25:147|AIH 7-3]].

quiz.q: Which item does 14 CFR 141.55 require in a part 141 training syllabus?
options: The fuel and oil used on each of the training flights
Each lesson's objectives, standards and planned time
A copy of each instructor's pilot certificate
The weather minimums for every training flight
quiz.why: The syllabus must include a detailed description of each lesson with its objectives, standards and planned time for completion, plus prerequisites, stage standards and stage checks [[60:785|14 CFR 141.55(c)(7)]]. None of the other items is on that list [[60:785|14 CFR 141.55(c)]].

quiz.q: A new CFII says, "I keep my lesson plans in my head." Which AIH point answers him best?
options: Another instructor should be able to teach from it
Written plans are needed only at part 141 schools
Written plans matter only for classroom lessons
That is fine as long as the lessons are one-on-one in flight
quiz.why: A mental outline is not a lesson plan. It should be written so another instructor could conduct the same period and so it can be checked for adequacy and completeness [[25:151|AIH 7-7]]. A plan should be prepared for each training period, flight or ground [[25:151|AIH 7-7]].

quiz.q: Which of these is one of the purposes of a lesson plan listed in the AIH?
options: Promote uniformity of instruction
Replace the syllabus under part 61
Let you skip the preflight briefing
Fix each lesson's length in advance
quiz.why: An adequate lesson plan should promote uniformity of instruction regardless of the instructor or the date, among seven purposes that include a wise selection of material and relating the lesson to the course objectives [[25:152|AIH 7-8]]. A good syllabus feeds the lesson plan; the plan does not replace it [[25:151|AIH 7-7]].

quiz.q: Your plan adds three new approach types plus holding in one lesson for an early-stage learner. Which characteristic of a well-planned lesson does it break?
options: Practicality
Flexibility
Relation to course
Scope
quiz.why: Each lesson should be reasonable in scope: a person can master only a few principles or skills at a time, and too much material results in confusion [[25:152|AIH 7-8]]. Practicality is about planning for the conditions and aids where the training happens [[25:152|AIH 7-8]].

quiz.q: Which three parts should every lesson plan format include, whatever it calls them?
options: Attention, motivation and an overview of the lesson
Objectives, content and completion standards
Preflight, flight and postflight discussion
Preparation, presentation and application
quiz.why: All lesson plans should include objectives, content to support them and completion standards, though completion standards may be called assessment, review and feedback or performance evaluation [[25:153|AIH 7-9]]. Attention, motivation and overview are the parts of a lesson introduction [[25:112|AIH 5-9]].

quiz.q: Before an SBT flight, which items does the AIH say the instructor and learner should establish?
options: Aircraft, fuel reserve, alternate and passenger count
Route, altitude, alternate and expected ATC clearance
Objective, grade sheet, endorsement and test date
Destination, outcomes, performance level and changes
quiz.why: For SBT to be effective, the instructor and learner establish the scenario destination(s), desired learning outcomes, desired level of learner performance and possible inflight scenario changes [[25:155|AIH 7-11]]. The learner also plans route, weather and NOTAMs, but those are not this list [[25:31|AIH 1-27]].

quiz.q: Your learner flies the planned SBT trip, decides to divert and lands safely. How should the postflight review start?
options: With your grade sheet and list of errors
With the learner's own self-critique
With a short quiz on the regulations
With a preview of the next lesson
quiz.why: The SBT postflight review should typically begin with learner self-critique, with the instructor leading through questions that generate reflective thinking [[25:156|AIH 7-12]]. Collaborative assessment then compares the self-assessment with the instructor's detailed assessment [[25:182|AIH 9-12]].

quiz.q: Your instrument-airplane syllabus must include a cross-country flight with an instructor under IFR. Which matches 14 CFR 61.65(d)?
options: 250 nautical miles, an approach at each airport, three kinds
100 nautical miles, one approach, any two kinds of approaches
250 nautical miles, an approach at the destination, one ILS
50 nautical miles, two approaches, one of them a GPS approach
quiz.why: The flight is 250 nautical miles along airways or ATC-directed routing, with an instrument approach at each airport and three different kinds of approaches using navigation systems [[60:251|14 CFR 61.65(d)(2)]]. The 100 nautical mile flight is the helicopter version [[60:252|14 CFR 61.65(e)(2)]].

final_quiz.q: Which statement about the ACS or PTS in a training course matches the AIH?
options: It covers critical tasks only, so it is not a whole syllabus
It is the complete syllabus for each certificate or rating
It sets the lesson order every instructor is required to follow
It replaces lesson completion standards entirely
final_quiz.why: ACS/PTS standards are limited to the most critical job tasks, and certification tests do not represent an entire training syllabus [[25:108|AIH 5-5]]. The ACS/PTS is a testing tool; lesson standards should gradually reach or exceed it before checkride preparation [[25:171|AIH 9-1]].

final_quiz.q: Which pair describes content validity and criterion validity for a test item?
options: Easy to give; scored the same by every grader
Covers all objectives; separates strong learners
Mimics real flying; standards fit real flight
New to the learner; done within a time limit
final_quiz.why: Content validity means a maneuver closely mimics what actual flying requires; criterion validity means its completion standards reflect acceptable standards in actual flight [[25:109|AIH 5-6]]. Usability, objectivity, comprehensiveness and discrimination are other test characteristics [[25:136|AIH 6-5]].

final_quiz.q: When should an instructor shift toward decision-based objectives?
options: Before the very first flight, to set the tone for the course
Only after the practical test is passed
Only for learners who had an incident
As the learner reaches higher performance levels
final_quiz.why: As the learner progresses through higher levels of performance and understanding, the instructor should shift the focus to decision-based objectives, which suit SBT and teach risk management and ADM [[25:108|AIH 5-5]]. Maneuver training does not stop; maneuvers are integrated into scenarios [[25:110|AIH 5-7]].

final_quiz.q: You listed the criteria for each of a lesson's objectives. According to the AIH, what else have you done?
options: Finished the course syllabus
Written the completion standards
Chosen the teaching method
Set the stage check date
final_quiz.why: By listing the criteria for the training objectives, the instructor has already established the completion standards normally included in the lesson plan [[25:110|AIH 5-7]]. Choosing the method is a separate step of the planning cycle [[25:152|AIH 7-8]].

final_quiz.q: Why does the building-block approach boost a learner's self-confidence?
options: Each block ends with an easy written quiz
Blocks let the learner skip hard material
Each finished block makes a big goal manageable
Blocks remove the need for any stage checks
final_quiz.why: A boost in self-confidence normally comes each time a block is completed, and smaller blocks make a goal that might seem unobtainable manageable [[25:146|AIH 7-2]]. Blocks are integral parts of the whole, not a way around hard material [[25:146|AIH 7-2]].

final_quiz.q: How does the IFH say the two fundamental skills of attitude instrument flying are learned?
options: Separately and in sequence, then integrated
Together from the first flight, never apart
In the airplane first, then in a device
Only after the knowledge test is passed
final_quiz.why: Instrument cross-check and instrument interpretation are learned separately and in deliberate sequence, and proficiency shows in integrating them into smooth, positive control [[23:143|IFH 6-10]]. The IFH lesson guide uses the building-block technique for the same reason [[23:342|IFH B-1]].

final_quiz.q: Which lesson opens the IFH Instrument Training Lesson Guide?
options: A demonstration of an ILS approach and a missed approach
An evaluation of the learner's knowledge and skill
Partial panel practice and unusual attitudes
A review of the instrument practical test
final_quiz.why: Lesson 1 is a ground and flight evaluation of the learner's knowledge and performance [[23:342|IFH B-1]]. Partial panel and unusual attitudes come in Lessons 6 and 7, and practical test preparation comes last [[23:343|IFH B-2]] [[23:344|IFH B-3]].

final_quiz.q: Compared with part 141 and 142 syllabi, what does the AIH say other syllabi may lack?
options: Lesson content and a list of maneuvers
Any reference to the regulations at all
Ground lessons to go with the flight lessons
Prerequisites, completion times and stage checks
final_quiz.why: Syllabi for training outside approved schools may not provide enrollment prerequisites, planned completion times, or descriptions of the checks and tests for each stage [[25:147|AIH 7-3]]. Part 141 requires those items [[60:785|14 CFR 141.55(c)(7)]].

final_quiz.q: What risk management should a flight training syllabus include?
options: Training unique to each stage, with subtler risks later
One risk briefing at the very start of the course
None; risk is covered only in ground school
A risk test just before the practical test
final_quiz.why: The flight training syllabus should include risk management instruction unique to each stage, phase or training element, and scenarios should include increasingly subtle risks [[25:149|AIH 7-5]].

final_quiz.q: Besides guiding training, what other use of a syllabus does the AIH describe?
options: A record that supports endorsements
A substitute for the learner's pilot logbook
Proof of airworthiness for each flight
A ready-made practical test for the examiner
final_quiz.why: A syllabus can be a checklist that required training is done, and its records serve as a basis for endorsements and recommendations for knowledge and practical tests [[25:150|AIH 7-6]].

final_quiz.q: In flight, your learner lacks an element essential to today's lesson. What may you do with the lesson plan?
options: Finish the plan exactly as written
End the lesson and reschedule it
Change it, or drop it for a review
Skip ahead to the next lesson's items
final_quiz.why: A flight lesson plan may have to be modified considerably in flight because of deficiencies in knowledge or poor mastery of essential elements, and in some cases abandoned in favor of review [[25:153|AIH 7-9]].

final_quiz.q: Which characteristic of a well-planned lesson calls for new material tied to earlier lessons, usually with a short review?
options: Unity
Scope
Flexibility
Content
final_quiz.why: Content: each lesson should contain new material related to the lesson before, and a short review of earlier lessons is usually needed, particularly in flight training [[25:152|AIH 7-8]]. Unity is about limited objectives that all the procedures serve [[25:152|AIH 7-8]].

final_quiz.q: What idea, called situated cognition, is SBT based on?
options: Facts must be memorized before any flying
Device skills never carry over to airplanes
Each learner has one fixed learning style
Knowledge cannot be understood apart from context
final_quiz.why: SBT is based on situated cognition: knowledge cannot be known and fully understood independent of its context, so people learn better from realistic situations where they are counted on to perform [[25:157|AIH 7-13]].

final_quiz.q: Which statement about traditional training and SBT matches Figure 7-8?
options: SBT should replace all maneuver training
Traditional training should come after SBT
Most solutions should use both of them
SBT is only for pilots with an instrument rating
final_quiz.why: Figure 7-8 says most learning solutions should employ both traditional training and SBT, and traditional elements should enhance the SBT elements [[25:157|AIH 7-13]]. Maneuvers that need repetition are still taught in concentrated settings [[25:154|AIH 7-10]].

final_quiz.q: Your scenario may lead the learner to divert for weather. What freedom does the AIH say the learner should have?
options: Only the outcome you planned is allowed
Good and poor choices, but no unsafe acts
Any choice, even an unsafe one, to learn
None; you make every decision in the flight
final_quiz.why: Understand in advance which outcomes are positive and negative and let the learner make both good and poor decisions, but never an unsafe decision or an unsafe act [[25:31|AIH 1-27]] [[25:120|AIH 5-17]].

final_quiz.q: In SBT, once your learner begins making the decisions on a flight, what role does the AIH say you take?
options: Examiner who grades each decision
Silent passenger who never speaks
Lead decision maker for the flight
Mentor and learning facilitator
final_quiz.why: The instructor keeps demonstrating and teaching skill maneuvers in the traditional way, but when the learner begins to make decisions, reverts to the role of mentor and learning facilitator [[25:155|AIH 7-11]]. The instructor should turn planning and execution over to the learner as soon as possible [[25:155|AIH 7-11]].

takeaways: Plan downhill: course objectives and standards first, then blocks, the syllabus, and one written lesson plan per period.
Write objectives with a measurable description, conditions and criteria; add decision-based objectives as the learner advances.
The ACS/PTS is a test, not a syllabus: aim past the minimums and teach why and when, not only how.
Build in blocks the learner can master and combine, starting from what this learner already knows.
A syllabus is a brief digest with lesson objectives, content and standards, stage standards and risk management, used as a flexible guide.
A lesson plan has objectives, content and completion standards, and shows unity, content, scope, practicality, flexibility, relation to the course and the teaching steps.
An SBT lesson starts with pre-scenario planning and a real reason to fly, has no single right answer, and closes with a postflight review that begins with the learner's self-critique.
cfi_notes: The PTS NOTE for Area I says the evaluator selects at least Tasks E, F and G and one other Task, so this Task is tested whenever Area I is [[FAA-S-8081-9E:23|PTS Area I NOTE]]. Under FAA-S-8081-9E, Area I is part of the test for an initial flight instructor instrument certificate, but the PTS table for adding an instrument instructor rating to a flight instructor certificate marks Area I as not required [[FAA-S-8081-9E:18|PTS Addition of an Instrument Instructor Rating]]. The PTS also lists knowledge of the development and effective use of a course of training, a syllabus and a lesson plan, including scenario-based training and collaborative assessment, among the items for satisfactory performance [[FAA-S-8081-9E:15|PTS Satisfactory Performance]], and the ability to develop scenario-based instruction that meets lesson objectives among the evaluator's checks [[FAA-S-8081-9E:13|PTS Evaluator Responsibility]].

Bring real plans. In Area IV (Maneuver Lesson) the PTS has you present a preflight lesson using a lesson plan, and previously developed plans from your library may be used [[FAA-S-8081-9E:30|PTS Area IV NOTE]]. The AIH says commercially developed lesson plans are acceptable for flight instructor applicants on practical tests, but should be adapted [[25:153|AIH 7-9]]. The CFII lesson FII.IV.A covers that Task.

Two wordings of the teaching steps: Chapter 5 names them preparation, presentation, application and assessment [[25:104|AIH 5-1]], while Chapter 7's characteristic of instructional steps says preparation, presentation, application, and review and evaluation [[25:153|AIH 7-9]]. They are the same four steps; use the examiner's wording.

The AIH gives three lists for a good scenario: five items in Chapter 5 [[25:120|AIH 5-17]], eight in Chapter 1, adding all three domains, interactive and time-pressured decisions [[25:31|AIH 1-27]], and three in Chapter 3: clear objectives, tailored to the learner, and using the local environment [[25:82|AIH 3-31]]. They do not conflict; know them as one picture.

The accident statement varies slightly: Chapter 5 says improper decisions cause the majority of fatal accidents in aircraft [[25:110|AIH 5-7]], while Chapter 7 says the majority of fatal accidents in light single- and twin-engine aircraft [[25:154|AIH 7-10]]. Quote the Chapter 7 wording for general aviation training.

The PTS references FAA-H-8083-9 [[FAA-S-8081-9E:25|PTS I.G]]; this lesson uses the 9B. Both the PHAK and the AIH call the test standard a testing document, not a training syllabus or teaching tool [[1:37|PHAK 1-22]] [[25:171|AIH 9-1]].

These planning skills carry over to IPCs. AC 61-98E tells the instructor to develop a plan of action that uses realistic scenarios to organize and sequence the IPC tasks [[15:31|AC 61-98E 5.1.3.3]], and the RMH says flight reviews and IPCs should use scenarios that address the hazards and risks relevant to the pilot [[30:59|RMH A-1]].

How it is tested: expect scenario questions such as "this learner has a different background" or "weather cancels the planned lesson". Answer in the AIH order (objectives and standards, blocks, syllabus, lesson plan, SBT) and give an instrument example each time, since the PTS asks evaluators to test application and correlation [[FAA-S-8081-9E:14|PTS Evaluator Responsibility]].
gaps: The Instrument Rating ACS gives the final numbers, for example altitude ±100 feet, selected headings ±10°, airspeed ±10 knots and bank angles ±5° in instrument flight [[FAA-S-ACS-8C:16|IR ACS IR.IV.A.S1]], and no more than ¾-scale CDI deflection, airspeed ±10 knots and MDA +100/-0 feet on a nonprecision final approach segment [[FAA-S-ACS-8C:21|IR ACS IR.VI.A.S12]]. The sample completion standards say "within the limits written for this stage"; take the final numbers from the ACS.

The AIH gives no complete instrument lesson plan or instrument SBT lesson plan. The instrument plans here are this lesson's own examples, built from the AIH formats [[25:154|AIH 7-10]] [[25:156|AIH 7-12]] and the IFH lesson guide [[23:342|IFH B-1]].

The IFH lesson guide lists topics only, with no objectives, completion standards or times per lesson [[23:342|IFH B-1]] [[23:344|IFH B-3]]. No source here says how many hours each instrument block should take; the IFH says the time needed depends on the individual's ability, not the regulation [[23:11|IFH viii]].
The AIH points to FAA generic syllabi, a generic transition syllabus and FITS web pages for more on SBT [[25:157|AIH 7-13]] [[25:158|AIH 7-14]]. Those documents are not in this lesson's sources.
No source here sets one required lesson plan format for the practical test; the AIH says formats and even the terms for the main headings vary [[25:153|AIH 7-9]].

activities.title: Description, conditions or criteria?
activities.intro: Each phrase comes from an instrument objective. Tap a phrase, then the part of a performance-based objective it belongs to.
buckets: Description of the skill or behavior

items.t: Intercept and track an assigned VOR radial
Enter and fly the holding pattern in the clearance
Explain why the missed approach point is where it is
In the training airplane, under a view-limiting device
Using the current en route and approach charts
With the attitude and heading indicators covered
Within the altitude limit written for this stage
Without instructor help on two tries in a row
Arriving at the fix within 1 minute of the planned time

activities.why: The description states the outcome in concrete, measurable terms; conditions give the equipment, tools, references and limits; criteria are the standards that leave no question whether the objective was met [[25:108|AIH 5-5]] [[25:109|AIH 5-6]]. The AIH's own criteria example uses a planned arrival time [[25:109|AIH 5-6]].

activities.title: The IFH instrument lessons, block by block
activities.intro: Put these lessons from the IFH Instrument Training Lesson Guide in their order, first to last, then tap Check.
steps: Ground and flight evaluation of the learner's knowledge and performance
Preflight preparation and flight by reference to instruments
Navigation systems: intercepting, tracking and holding
activities.why: Lessons 1, 2, 4, 6, 7, 8, 20 and 21, and 24 and later of the IFH guide, arranged in a logical sequence with the building-block technique [[23:342|IFH B-1]] [[23:343|IFH B-2]] [[23:344|IFH B-3]].

activities.title: In the part 141 syllabus, or elsewhere in the course?
activities.intro: 14 CFR 141.55(c) lists what an approved course must contain. Sort each item: is it part of the training syllabus itself, or another part of the course?

items.t: Prerequisites for enrolling in the ground and flight portions
Each lesson's objectives, standards and planned time
What the course should accomplish in student learning
Expected accomplishments and standards for each stage
Checks and tests that measure each stage
Each ground training room and how many students it holds
Each flight simulator or flight training device used
Airports where training flights start, and their facilities
Minimum qualifications and ratings of each instructor

activities.why: The syllabus items are in 141.55(c)(7); rooms, devices, airports and instructor qualifications are in 141.55(c)(1) to (6) [[60:785|14 CFR 141.55(c)]]. The AIH notes that syllabi outside approved schools may lack prerequisites, completion times and stage checks [[25:147|AIH 7-3]].

activities.title: True or false: using a syllabus
activities.intro: Decide if each statement is true or false.

cards.s: Under part 61, the syllabus order should never change once training starts.
cards.why: False. Under part 61 the order of training can and should be altered to suit the learner's progress and special circumstances [[25:147|AIH 7-3]].

cards.s: At a certificated school, compliance with the approved syllabus is a condition for graduation.
cards.why: True. Both the instructor and the learner should have a copy [[25:147|AIH 7-3]].

cards.s: A syllabus should adapt to weather, aircraft availability and scheduling changes.
cards.why: True, without disrupting the teaching process or suspending training [[25:147|AIH 7-3]].

cards.s: Most syllabi introduce a maneuver once and never return to it.
cards.why: False. Most introduce each procedure or maneuver in one lesson and review it in later lessons [[25:150|AIH 7-6]].

cards.s: Syllabus records can serve as a basis for endorsements and test recommendations.
Part 61 spells out exactly how instrument training must be organized.
cards.why: False. Part 61 sets the minimum experience and knowledge training but does not stipulate how training is organized [[1:34|PHAK 1-19]].

cards.s: A well-constructed syllabus already holds much of what a lesson plan needs.
cards.why: True: objectives, content and completion standards [[25:151|AIH 7-7]].

cards.s: A learner's training records should be kept for at least 3 years.
cards.why: True, per the AIH's guidance on the training folder [[25:152|AIH 7-8]].

activities.title: The planning cycle for one lesson
activities.intro: Put the AIH's planning steps in order, first to last, then tap Check.
steps: Research the subject as the objective defines it
Identify a useful lesson planning format
Decide how to organize the lesson and select support material
activities.why: The complete cycle of planning from [[25:152|AIH 7-8]]. One technique is to write the beginning and ending of the outline first, then complete it and revise as required [[25:152|AIH 7-8]].

activities.title: Which characteristic is missing?
activities.intro: Tap each weak lesson plan, then the characteristic of a well-planned lesson it lacks.

pairs.l: Partial panel, a new approach type and a weather talk, with no common goal
Nothing in it connects to what the learner flew last time
Four new procedures packed into one hour for an early learner
A classroom plan used unchanged for a lesson in the airplane
No room to add anything if the learner needs more
The learner cannot say why the lesson matters for the rating or for safety

activities.why: The characteristics of a well-planned lesson from [[25:152|AIH 7-8]] and [[25:153|AIH 7-9]]. The seventh, instructional steps, means the lesson follows preparation, presentation, application, and review and evaluation [[25:153|AIH 7-9]].

activities.title: Planning Mia's instrument course, one decision at a time
activities.intro: You are the CFII for Mia, a private pilot who wants an instrument rating to fly her family to the coast. Make each planning call as her training unfolds.

steps.s: First meeting. Mia hands you a printout of the instrument rating ACS and says, "Let's just practice these until I pass."
options: Agree, and use the ACS task list as her lesson order
Explain the ACS is a test standard, and build a syllabus
Say a syllabus is needed only at part 141 schools
Start flying approaches today and plan the course later
steps.why: The ACS/PTS is a testing tool, not a teaching tool [[25:171|AIH 9-1]], and certification tests do not represent an entire training syllabus [[25:108|AIH 5-5]]. The PHAK says unorganized part 61 training can cost time and money through repetition, and a well-documented training syllabus is one way to avoid it [[1:34|PHAK 1-19]].

steps.s: You draft her stage 1 objective: "Mia will understand partial panel flying."
options: Keep it, since understanding is the goal of the stage
Add only a list of the instruments that will be covered
Replace it with the date the stage should be finished
Rewrite it with measurable behavior, conditions, criteria
steps.why: Performance-based objectives need a description in concrete, measurable terms, conditions and criteria [[25:108|AIH 5-5]] [[25:109|AIH 5-6]].

steps.s: Her logbook shows strong VFR navigation with a GPS navigator, but almost no hood time.
options: Start at the guide's Lesson 1 and build on what she knows
Skip the attitude blocks, since she flies the GPS well
Begin with full approaches so she sees the end goal
Put all ground lessons first, then all flight lessons
steps.why: Learn her background and plan blocks that build on it [[25:147|AIH 7-3]]. The IFH guide starts with an evaluation and builds attitude instrument skills before navigation and approaches, pairing ground training with each flight lesson [[23:342|IFH B-1]] [[23:343|IFH B-2]].

steps.s: On the day of her first partial panel flight, low clouds and icing make the airplane lesson unwise.
options: Cancel her training for the week until it clears
Fly anyway, since real weather is good training
Teach the same block on the ground and in the device
Jump ahead to the cross-country lessons instead
steps.why: A syllabus should adapt to weather without suspending training [[25:147|AIH 7-3]], and instrument tasks can first be taught in an FFS, FTD or ATD [[25:174|AIH 9-4]].

steps.s: Mid-course she flies partial panel well in the practice area. You want to see her use it on a real trip.
options: Repeat the practice-area drill until it is perfect
Build an SBT trip to the coast with a possible failure
Fail an instrument by surprise on a low short final
Move on, since partial panel is done to standard
steps.why: Present the maneuver objectives in a scenario, with learned maneuvers integrated into realistic flight [[25:154|AIH 7-10]] [[25:155|AIH 7-11]]. A good scenario is not a test and should not promote errors [[25:120|AIH 5-17]].

steps.s: After the SBT flight, Mia is quiet. How do you open the debrief?
options: Read her your list of errors from the flight first
Grade her quickly and preview the next lesson
Skip the debrief, since the flight went well
Ask her to replay the flight and assess it herself
steps.why: The postflight review typically begins with learner self-critique [[25:156|AIH 7-12]]; the instructor asks the learner to replay the flight, then reconstruct, reflect and redirect [[25:136|AIH 6-5]] [[25:137|AIH 6-6]].
